name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
summary: Leibniz, in political writings for German princes and the Empire, grounded justice in reason and the charity of the wise, rejected arbitrary power in kings and assemblies alike, favoured a balanced government and preventing poverty over relieving it, and attacked Louis XIV's pursuit of universal monarchy.

notes: First audit. Read by theme in the Riley edition of Leibniz's Political Writings (justice, sovereignty, forms of government, poverty and property, war and peace, the Mars Christianissimus satire on Louis XIV and the Observations on the Abbe de Saint-Pierre's perpetual peace) and, in the Theodicy, the preliminary dissertation on faith and reason, toleration and punishment. Riley's introduction and the Mars Christianissimus satire (written ironically in the voice of a flatterer of Louis XIV) were not cited as his positions. Searched without a settled answer: perpetual peace and international tribunals (he doubted Saint-Pierre's federal scheme and favoured a purified medieval Christian order, half in jest), toleration (he favoured reunion of the churches but states no general law), torture, and war (he treats war as sometimes necessary but condemns pursuit of universal monarchy by violence). Most statements are modern and stay null.
